name: John
author: Christians have traditionally held that this Gospel was written by John, son of Zebedee, a fisherman from Galilee who became one of Jesus' twelve closest followers. The book itself points to an unnamed 'disciple whom Jesus loved' as its eyewitness source. Many scholars think it was written down by a follower or a circle of followers of that disciple, or by another early Christian leader named John, drawing on his testimony.
audience: Early tradition places its first readers around Ephesus, a large city in what is now western Turkey, though this is not certain. They seem to have been a mix of Jewish and non-Jewish believers. The writer explains Jewish customs and translates Hebrew and Aramaic words, so not every reader knew them. Some may have been pushed out of their local synagogues for following Jesus.
era: The events take place around AD 30, when Judea was under Roman rule through the governor Pontius Pilate and Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas. The Gospel was most likely written around AD 90, a generation later, though some suggest an earlier date. By then the Romans had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70. Jewish communities were rebuilding without the temple, and tensions between synagogues and followers of Jesus were growing.

notes.1:1: This opening, often called the prologue, uses 'the Word' (Greek logos), a term familiar both to Jewish readers and to Greek thinkers of the day.
notes.2:1: Village weddings could last several days, and the host family was expected to keep guests supplied; running out of wine would have been a real embarrassment.
notes.2:12: Passover was the spring festival remembering Israel's escape from Egypt, drawing huge crowds of pilgrims to Jerusalem. Here John places the temple clearing early; the other Gospels place it near the end.
notes.3:1: Pharisees were a respected Jewish group devoted to careful keeping of God's law; Nicodemus also sat on the ruling council in Jerusalem.
notes.4:1: Jews and Samaritans had been bitterly divided for centuries over worship and ancestry; Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, near Jacob's well, rather than in Jerusalem.
notes.4:46: The royal official was most likely in the service of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee under Rome.
notes.5:1: Archaeologists have uncovered a large pool complex near Jerusalem's Sheep Gate, widely identified as Bethesda, matching the description of pools surrounded by covered walkways.
notes.6:1: The Sea of Galilee was also called the Sea of Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore in honour of the Emperor Tiberius.
notes.7:1: The Festival of Tabernacles, or Booths, was an autumn harvest celebration when families lived in temporary shelters, remembering Israel's years in the wilderness.
notes.7:37: Later Jewish writings describe priests carrying water from the Pool of Siloam each day of this festival and pouring it out at the temple altar.
notes.7:53: This story does not appear in the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, and many Bibles mark it off; it was likely an early account added later.
notes.8:12: During Tabernacles, great lamps were lit in the temple courts, reportedly lighting up much of Jerusalem; the treasury was in this same area.
notes.8:48: The Pool of Siloam lay in the southern part of Jerusalem; its remains were rediscovered by archaeologists in 2004.
notes.10:22: The Festival of Dedication, now called Hanukkah, remembered the temple's rededication in 164 BC after Jewish rebels freed it from a foreign king who had defiled it.
notes.11:45: Caiaphas served as high priest from about AD 18 to 36, holding office with Roman approval; the council was the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's highest Jewish court.
notes.12:12: Palm branches had been a symbol of Jewish national hope and victory since the Jewish revolt against foreign rule in the 160s BC.
notes.12:20: These Greeks were probably non-Jews who worshipped Israel's God and had come to Jerusalem for the Passover festival.
notes.13:1: Washing guests' dusty feet was normally a servant's task. John sets this meal just before Passover, a timing that differs slightly from the other Gospels.
notes.18:1: The garden lay across the Kidron Valley on the Mount of Olives; the other Gospels call it Gethsemane.
notes.18:12: Annas had been high priest around AD 6 to 15 and, as Caiaphas's father-in-law, remained a powerful figure in the priestly family.
notes.18:28: Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36; under Roman rule, Jewish leaders could not carry out executions themselves.
notes.19:17: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and criminals, carried out publicly outside city walls as a warning to others.
notes.19:38: Wealthy families buried their dead in tombs cut into rock, wrapping the body in linen with spices; the amount described here was lavish.
notes.21:1: Many scholars think this final chapter was added as an epilogue, possibly by the author's circle, after the book's first ending.
notes.21:20: The closing verses, partly written as 'we', suggest the author's community added them, possibly after the beloved disciple's death, to address a rumour about him.

flags.problem: The Pool of Siloam does not appear at 8:48. It first appears in the healing of the man born blind in chapter 9 (around 9:7), so the note is attached to the wrong passage and would confuse readers. The fact itself (rediscovered in 2004) is correct.

The claim that Jewish leaders could not carry out executions under Roman rule is stated as settled fact. Historians debate how absolute this restriction was; the stoning of Stephen and the execution of James in AD 62 are often raised against it.
flags.suggestion: Soften it, e.g. 'Rome generally kept the power of execution in the governor's hands, though historians debate how strictly this applied.'

flags.problem: Authorship of the closing verses is presented one-sidedly. The note gives only the view that the author's community added them, possibly after the beloved disciple's death, and leaves out the traditional view that the author wrote them himself.
flags.suggestion: Add a short clause such as 'Traditionally they have been read as the author's own words; many scholars think his community added them…'
